Simandou Mining Summit: Mamadi Doumbouya lance l’appel qui va consacrer le réveil économique de la Guinée
items.description: Avec le Simandou Mining Sommit prévu du 11 au 14 novembre à Conakry la Guinée a décidé de frachir un nouveau cape dans sa conquête du monde des affaires. C’est pourquoi, dans une publication officielle pour la circonstance, en prélude à cet événement d'envergure, le président de la République déclare que: «Le monde a rendez-vous en République de Guinée. » Une phrase courte, mais vibrante, qui sonne comme une invitation solennelle autant que comme la réaffirmation du leadership retrouvé sur la scène économique continentale. En tout cas, «Le 11 novembre 2026, sur l’île de Kassa, s’ouvrira la 𝟭ʳᵉ 𝗲́𝗱𝗶𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗱𝘂 𝗦𝗶𝗺𝗮𝗻𝗱𝗼𝘂 𝗠𝗶𝗻𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗦𝘂𝗺𝗺𝗶𝘁, placée sous le thème : « 𝗟’𝗶𝗻𝗱𝘂𝘀𝘁𝗿𝗶𝗲 𝗺𝗶𝗻𝗶𝗲̀𝗿𝗲, 𝗺𝗼𝘁𝗲𝘂𝗿 𝗱𝗲 𝗹𝗮 𝗱𝗶𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘀𝗶𝗳𝗶𝗰𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗲́𝗰𝗼𝗻𝗼𝗺𝗶𝗾𝘂𝗲 𝗮̀ 𝗹’𝗲̀𝗿𝗲 𝗱𝗲 𝗦𝗶𝗺𝗮𝗻𝗱𝗼𝘂 𝟮𝟬𝟰𝟬 », rappelle-t-il. Poursuivant son message, le chef de l’Etat note «qu’il y a un an, Simandou entrait en exploitation». Et «qu’Aujourd’hui, la Guinée franchit une nouvelle étape : 𝘁𝗿𝗮𝗻𝘀𝗳𝗼𝗿𝗺𝗲𝗿 𝘀𝗲𝘀 𝗿𝗲𝘀𝘀𝗼𝘂𝗿𝗰𝗲𝘀 𝗲𝗻 𝗶𝗻𝗱𝘂𝘀𝘁𝗿𝗶𝗲𝘀, 𝗲𝗻 𝗲𝗺𝗽𝗹𝗼𝗶𝘀 𝗲𝘁 𝗲𝗻 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝘀𝗽𝗲́𝗿𝗶𝘁𝗲́ 𝗽𝗮𝗿𝘁𝗮𝗴𝗲́𝗲». C’est pourquoi, explique l’actuel locateur du palais Mohamed V, «j’𝗶𝗻𝘃𝗶𝘁𝗲 𝗹𝗲𝘀 𝗶𝗻𝘃𝗲𝘀𝘁𝗶𝘀𝘀𝗲𝘂𝗿𝘀, 𝗹𝗲𝘀 𝗽𝗮𝗿𝘁𝗲𝗻𝗮𝗶𝗿𝗲𝘀 𝗲𝘁 𝗹𝗲𝘀 𝗮𝗺𝗶𝘀 𝗱𝗲 𝗹𝗮 𝗚𝘂𝗶𝗻𝗲́𝗲 𝗮̀ 𝘃𝗲𝗻𝗶𝗿 𝗰𝗼𝗻𝘀𝘁𝗮𝘁𝗲𝗿 𝗽𝗮𝗿 𝗲𝘂𝘅-𝗺𝗲̂𝗺𝗲𝘀 𝗹𝗮 𝗻𝗼𝘂𝘃𝗲𝗹𝗹𝗲 𝗱𝘆𝗻𝗮𝗺𝗶𝗾𝘂𝗲 𝗱𝗲 𝗱𝗲́𝘃𝗲𝗹𝗼𝗽𝗽𝗲𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁 de notre pays». Et de terminier son message par la formule percutante, « GUINEA IS OPEN FOR BUSINESS », le président Doumbouya tend la main pour un partenariat pupblic privé gagant gagant dans une Guinée résolument tournée vers l'avenir.

items.title: ADAMU: Like father, Amos, like son, Samson, by Patrick Omorodion
items.description: Recently, the Confederation of African Football, CAF confirmed Samson Adamu, the scion of Dr. Amos Adamu, as the General Secretary of the continental football body. Former Super Eagles player, Paul Okoku in today’s Column takes a peep into the rise of the younger Adamu in African football and states that his appointment should “encourage Nigeria to invest more seriously in developing qualified sports administrators, coaches, technical professionals and former athletes interested in leadership”. Enjoy it! SAMSON ADAMU MAKES HISTORY AT CAF: BEYOND THE CONGRATULATIONS, WHAT COMES NEXT? Nigeria has another reason to celebrate an important milestone in African football administration. Samson Adamu has reportedly been confirmed as the substantive General Secretary of the Confederation of African Football (CAF), becoming the first Nigerian to occupy the position since the organisation’s establishment in 1957. Congratulations are appropriate. But beyond the celebrations lies a more important question: What prepares an individual for such enormous responsibility, and what should African football expect from his leadership? An appointment makes history. Performance determines its legacy. A CAREER BUILT BEYOND THE HEADLINES Samson Adamu is not arriving at the summit of African football administration without professional preparation. He studied Business Management and Computer Science at the American University of Paris and completed the prestigious FIFA Master postgraduate programme in 2009. Before joining CAF, he spent approximately a decade with Kinetic Sport Management, where he helped develop Copa Lagos, an international beach soccer competition. His professional journey subsequently took him to CAF in 2018, where he served as Director of Competitions and later Director of Tournaments and Events. On March 29, 2026, he became Acting General Secretary following the departure of Véron Mosengo-Omba. These are relevant qualifications and experiences that deserve recognition. His career also demonstrates something Nigerian football frequently overlooks: successful sports administration requires specialised education, operational competence, strategic planning and institutional experience. AFCON’S RETURN TO EVERY TWO YEARS: SAMSON ADAMU’S ROLE One of the most significant recent developments in African football is CAF’s decision to reverse its controversial proposal to stage the Africa Cup of Nations every four years. On October 29, 2026, CAF’s Executive Committee unanimously approved the continuation of AFCON’s traditional two-year cycle, reversing the direction announced in December 2025. The decision was important for African football’s identity, commercial interests and the opportunities available to national teams, players and participating countries. But there is an interesting connection to Samson Adamu. According to Uganda’s Daily Monitor, Adamu, then serving as Acting CAF General Secretary, issued an official communication dated October 23, 2026, asking all 54 CAF member associations to submit recommendations on whether AFCON should be held every two or four years. The request came from CAF President Dr. Patrice Motsepe, with responses requested by October 28. This places Adamu directly within the administrative consultation process preceding the Executive Committee’s decision. The reversal itself was taken by CAF’s Executive Committee, not by Adamu individually. Nevertheless, the episode illustrates the substantial responsibilities attached to the General Secretary’s office and the importance of ensuring that member associations have opportunities to contribute to decisions affecting the continent’s football future. CAF has confirmed that the next tournaments will take place in 2027, 2028, 2031 and 2033, with no tournament scheduled for the 2030 FIFA World Cup year. For Samson Adamu, this is an early example of the governance challenges associated with his position. African football needs administrators capable of supporting transparent consultations, respecting member associations and implementing decisions that protect the continent’s sporting and economic interests. Leadership is not only about making decisions. It is also about ensuring that the voices of those affected are heard. THE FAMILY NAME AND THE INDIVIDUAL Samson is the son of Dr. Amos Adamu, one of Nigeria’s most influential former sports administrators. His father occupied senior positions in Nigerian sports administration and served on the executive committees of both CAF and FIFA. That family connection is part of Samson’s biography. It neither establishes his professional competence nor diminishes the qualifications he has independently acquired. A father’s achievements cannot automatically become his son’s achievements. Equally, a father’s mistakes cannot automatically become his son’s mistakes. The responsible approach is to assess Samson Adamu on his education, professional record, decisions and eventual performance in office. WHAT SHOULD AFRICAN FOOTBALL EXPECT? The CAF General Secretary is not merely a ceremonial representative. The office carries substantial administrative responsibility for an organisation serving 54 national football associations. Its work influences competitions, administration, institutional coordination and the implementation of decisions affecting African football. For Samson Adamu, the real examination now begins. Will CAF demonstrate greater administrative transparency? Will competition management become more consistent? Will the concerns of smaller football associations receive appropriate attention? Will institutional accountability become stronger? These are reasonable expectations of the office, not prejudgments against its new occupant. His appointment should also encourage Nigeria to invest more seriously in developing qualified sports administrators, coaches, technical professionals and former athletes interested in leadership. Our football institutions should provide transparent pathways through which competence, experience and integrity determine advancement. The emergence of one Nigerian at CAF should inspire opportunity for many others. HISTORY IS ONLY THE BEGINNING I congratulate Samson Adamu on this historic professional achievement and wish him wisdom, courage and success in serving African football. Nigeria should celebrate its citizens who distinguish themselves internationally. But celebration must never replace thoughtful assessment of responsibility. The highest honour of leadership is not simply reaching an important office. It is leaving the institution stronger, fairer and more credible than one found it. Samson Adamu has earned a place in African football history. What he does with that place will determine his legacy. The post ADAMU: Like father, Amos, like son, Samson, by Patrick Omorodion appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: BoG Governor Johnson Asiama says professional journalism is vital in fighting digital misinformation
items.description: Bank of Ghana Governor, Dr Johnson Pandit Asiama, has described professional journalism as “society’s compass”, saying it remains essential in helping citizens navigate the growing challenges of the digital age. Speaking at the 30th Ghana Journalists Association (GJA) Media Awards in Accra on Saturday, November 7, 2026, he said technological advancements had transformed how information is created, distributed and consumed, presenting both opportunities and challenges for society. Dr Asiama noted that while digital platforms had expanded opportunities for citizens to participate in public discussions and share information, they had also contributed to the spread of misinformation, disinformation, online abuse, misleading data and hate speech. “Although digital platforms have created unprecedented opportunities for citizens to get involved and share information, they have also brought significant challenges, including misinformation, disinformation, online abuse, misleading data and hate speech,” he said. The Governor said professional journalism plays a critical role in helping citizens distinguish facts from falsehood, evidence from speculation and informed analysis from sensationalism. He described journalists as guardians of public discourse whose work contributes to social cohesion, informed debate and the protection of democratic principles. “As guardians of public discourse, journalists are essential for building social unity, encouraging well-informed discussions, and safeguarding democratic principles,” he stated. Dr Asiama also highlighted the media’s role in making complex economic and financial issues accessible to the public. He cited monetary policy decisions, inflation trends, financial sector reforms, exchange rate movements and digital financial innovations as issues that require accurate and balanced reporting to help citizens understand developments affecting their lives. He said effective journalism translates such technical subjects into information that the public can understand and use. The 30th GJA Media Awards were held under the theme, “Celebrating Excellence, Advancing Media Freedom and Combating Hate Speech in the Digital Age”. The theme highlights the need to protect press freedom while promoting responsible journalism in an increasingly digital information environment. The Bank of Ghana has also pledged to continue supporting initiatives that recognise excellence in economic and financial reporting.

items.title: Institutional Memory, Professional Knowledge and the CORFEPS Journal
items.description: By Tunji Olaopa The Council of Retired Federal Permanent Secretaries (CORFEPS) is an association of patriotic former public servants that embodies administrative experiences, institutional memories and professional knowledge that could pull a lot of political and administrative weight within the reform imperative to transform governance architecture, the civil service and its ecosystem. As a multidisciplinary body of retired public servants with vast knowledge of the workings of the system, CORFEPS possesses a huge significance in connecting the institutional and reform dots in terms of where the civil service system is coming from, where it is at the moment and where it intends to be, given the democratic imperatives and development necessities of the current Tinubu administration. It is one of the most critical stakeholders in the public administration communities of practice and service that articulates a continuing professional and institutional interest in furthering the relevance of the civil service as a significant player in the development process in Nigeria. The necessity of such a body derives from the fact that patriotic and meritorious service does not need to end with retirement. Indeed, more can still be done in entrenching the institutional memories that retired permanent secretaries embody. CORFEPS, under the able chairmanship of Mahmud Yayale Ahmed, has been energetic in its consistent push to regain the vocational honor, professional ethos and administrative efficiency of the civil service. And in furtherance of this enthusiastic push for the significance of the civil service system as one critical cornerstone of democratic governance in Nigeria, CORFEPS has just launched an amazing initiative: the CORFEPS Journal on Pubic Policy and Governance. This significant initiative must be situated within a larger context of the institutional reform of the civil service system, especially its status as a value-based institution founded on merit, public spiritedness and professionalism. That context facilitates a framework that allows the past and the present to initiate conversation, and for both retired and current public servants to incessantly brainstorm the future of the bureaucratic system and its capability readiness to shoulder the burden of public policy implementation. The journal, I must say, presses the advantage of escalating the fundamental significance of professional knowledge and its role in deepening institutional progress. In other words, through it, CORFEPS provides a rare forum—draw, I dare say, from the administrative history of that golden era when administrative theorists (the gown) and practitioners (the town) were in conversation—within which administrative ideas, practices and initiatives could be discussed, extended and applied. The inaugural edition of the CORFEPS journal is indeed a full, rich and exciting package that is sufficiently exciting to signal to the communities of service and practice that something new and challenging has arrived in the administrative space. This is because the editorial board went all out to create a splash especially with the range of topics covered, and even more specially with the array of contributors and their unique specialties. As is to be expected, CORFEPS pulled strongly from within its own ranks for reflections that combine past administrative experiences with current observations from behind the scenes. The majority of the contributors are retired permanent secretaries who have served in one capacity or the other, and who have faced one crucial challenge or the other with wide ranging levels of successes. In this regard, the CORFEPS journal, in its inaugural edition, is drawing on the immense institutional memories and professional knowledge of its members to ventilate both diagnostic, recuperative and reformative insights. And this is salutary in ways that serve to complement the mediatory role CORFEPS has been playing as a staunch and energetic stakeholder in the civil service reform project in Nigeria. We now have an opportunity to listen and take note, outside of the usual high-power meetings, of the single-minded understanding of the civil service system from those who have manned its various aspects, especially the ministries, departments and agencies. Their reflections and analyses are complemented by others, critical watchers of the civil service, whose many years of dealing with the system make them significant participants in the ongoing efforts to transform it into a value-based, public-spirited, meritocratic and high-performing world class institution. Topics In terms of the range of topics and themes discussed in the inaugural edition, the CORFEPS journal becomes an automatic administrative keepsake. The inaugural edition is divided into eight parts. Each of the segments, with the exception of the last two, speaks intentionally to the most dominant issues involved in assessing and transforming Nigeria’s democratic governance experiment. This is indeed a well-thought out scholarly first step by the editorial board. Part one, titled “The Nigerian Civil Service,” has four essays; part two with seven essays is concerned with governance tools; part three has just one essay dealing with Nigeria’s infrastructural development; part four has two essays surrounding leadership and management; the two essays in part five are wrapped around the theme of health and lifestyle; part six is dedicated to three book reviews; part seven signals recent appointments and tributes to distinguished former public servants; and part eight speaks to the activities of CORFEPS itself. In all, these thematic segments are all-encompassing. They are meant to lay on the table the diagnoses, prognoses and resolution frameworks for understanding the totality of Nigeria’s administrative and governance challenges and the ways forward to transcending them. Without daring any in-depth review of each essay—which goes beyond the space of this piece—I will touch on some of the significant contributions. And of course, we start with the civil service system. This is key, even to the current advocacy responsibilities of CORFEPS itself. And the four essays in this segment did not disappoint. Their different focuses are without doubt current and contemporary—the status of the public administrator within the civil service and governance framework; the relationship between the civil service and the task of nation building; the significance of the MDAs in the achievement of state capacity; and the relationship between administrative leadership and performance management system. These are issues that are critical in reflecting on the challenges the civil service system is facing—how can we instigate the emergence of a public manager with twenty-first competences and literacies who can supervise a civil service system that is flexible, agile, technology-based and result-oriented through performance management that transforms Nigeria’s productivity? In the second segment of the journal, containing the most essays, the contributors engaged with governance matters that richly scope the depth of the key issues. I am particularly thrilled by the essays that investigate (a) public financial management and development financing, (b) the intervention of the executive in the institutional autonomy of public institutions, (c) decentralization and local governance, (d) capacity development to achieve service delivery and (e) the significance of corporate governance in the public sector. These issues connect with the earlier one on the administrative system. Budgeting and the financial management discipline that must attend it are critical for servicing development planning. And this goes beyond merely increasing budget size to the fundamentals of ensuring transparency and accountability in financing and execution that speaks to sustainable outcomes. I am also fascinated, as my many public interventions have demonstrated, with the place of local governance in Nigeria’s democratic governance. This also ties with the concern with the health of fiscal federalism in the Nigerian federation. Indeed, the author of the essay argues that constitutional autonomy to back the essence of local governance will be grossly less than optimal. Rather, what is needed is what he calls the “Nigeria Local Governance Reform Framework (2026-2035)” meant to reposition the local governments as key drivers of grassroots development. This is right on point. Similarly, the authors of the essay on training and capacity development attempt to recuperate training programmes “as genuine capacity-building instrument, anchored on competency-based needs assessment, transparent procurement, post-training accountability and the professionalization of Nigeria’s training institutions.” The third and fourth segments of the journal are tied together by the relationship between leadership and sustainable development. Sound leadership is the difference between successful and failed infrastructure projects. This then directs critical reform attention to the issue of leadership training and selection, the focus of the first essay in part four. Part five would seem to be off the path of a direct focus on administrative and governance subject matters in its focus on health and lifestyle. But that is not the case. Most reform blueprints, unlike the practice during the golden era of the public service in the 1970s, fail to factor in work-life balance in human capital development. This is crucial in the sense that when the public servant is healthy, it goes a long way in affecting performance and productivity. Thus, the two chapters on breast cancer and prostate health are key factor in institutional reform. Reform To recapitulate: the inaugural edition of the CORFEPS journal is really a mouthful! It is like a reader on institutional and governance reform that all MDAs and key parastatals must have in their libraries. More than this, the edition already raises the bar that the editorial board cannot afford to undermine, going forward. I have a series of recommendations in this regard. One, the journal must not attempt to be academic. It must rather be styled and intended as a journal for public administration and public service professionals. This then demands that the editorial board must give deep reflection, again, to the objective of the journal and its intended audience. The fundamental question in this sense would be: What does the CORFEPS journal aim to become in the next five years within the Nigerian communities of service and practice? This question impacts the idea of style and content. For example, every edition could then be themed around some specific subject matter of administrative and institutional reform, governance challenge, democratic consolidation, leadership, financial management, civil service mentoring, etc. Contributions can then be sourced from seasoned experts, public servants, administrators, while online search can also be made for syndicated columnists with innovative ideas and initiatives that speaks to the concerns of the journals. Indeed, special editions can be proposed on any theme for which the guest editor is renowned. Departments of public administration, as well as the MDAs, could serve as key studies for reflection on the overall health of the civil service system and public administration in Nigeria. Websites of other professional bodies will serve as veritable source of publishable materials to introduce new ideas, tools, techniques, etc. Young mentees, volunteers and analysts could also be enlisted and commissioned to write features on some current affairs that are relevant to public administration. Interviews and autobiographical notes are critical elements for understanding the progress and reform of the public service. The editorial board must therefore also think of segmenting the journals to give room for special features, from interviews to critical reform highlights in some of the MDAs. I will end this piece with a note of deep appreciation of those who thought the idea of the journal into existence. This is no mean feat in the total scheme of things concerning institutional reform in Nigerian civil service system. Kudos, first, to Alhaji M. Yayale Ahmed, the National Chairman of CORFEPS and the distinguished publisher of the journal. And then to Ambassador Dr Godknows Igali as the chair of the editorial board. I recognize every member of the editorial board and commend the efforts that went into birthing this inaugural edition. We have commenced a journey into a legacy of reform activities. *Olaopa, a retired Federal Permanent Secretary, is the Chairman, Federal Civil Service Commission, Abuja The post Institutional Memory, Professional Knowledge and the CORFEPS Journal appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Egypt sacks coach Hossam Hassan over ‘negative impact’ on team image
items.description: Egypt coach Hossam Hassan was sacked on Saturday for what the soccer federation cited as “a negative impact on the positive image of the team.” The Egyptian Football Association did not elaborate in a statement, adding only that “maintaining the team’s stability is a paramount priority” that cannot be compromised. Egyptian media believed the decision had more to do with Hassan’s personal life than rumors of disagreements with Egyptian players, including star forward Mohamed Salah. Egypt’s Supreme Council for Media Regulation banned Hassan last week from appearing in all media outlets, an unprecedented decision against a national coach. That followed disputes in Hassan’s personal life becoming public. Hassan was appointed Egypt coach in 2024 and became the first former Egypt player to coach the national team at a World Cup this year. Egypt was knocked out by Argentina in the last 16. The EFA immediately replaced Hassan with Ali Maher, a long-time head coach in the Egyptian Premier League currently leading fourth-placed Ceramica Cleopatra. Maher must get quickly up to speed. Egypt plays Malawi on Nov. 13 and 17 in qualifying for the 2027 Africa Cup of Nations. Egypt leads Group B.

items.title: BoG introduces economic and financial journalism award with international training opportunities at 30th GJA Media Awards
items.description: The Bank of Ghana (BoG) has announced a new award scheme to recognise excellence in economic and financial journalism, offering winners opportunities for international exposure, professional training and further studies. The Governor’s Economic and Financial Story of the Year Award was announced by Bank of Ghana Governor, Dr Johnson Pandit Asiama, in a speech he personally delivered at the 30th Ghana Journalists Association (GJA) Media Awards at the Palms Convention Centre, La Palm Royal Beach Hotel, Accra, on Saturday, November 7, 2026. The package includes sponsorship for the winner to attend either the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and World Bank Spring Meetings or Annual Meetings, a laptop computer and a one-year internet data subscription. It will also provide access to professional fellowships with institutions such as the Thomson Foundation, the Reuters Institute for the Study of Journalism and accredited local journalism training centres. Other opportunities include scholarships for further studies in media, communications and related fields, as well as professional exchange programmes with international media organisations such as Bloomberg and Reuters. “Our objective is simple: to invest in the development of journalists who can continue to elevate the quality of economic and financial reporting in Ghana,” the Governor said. The Governor described the media as an essential partner in helping the public understand economic and financial developments. He noted that issues such as monetary policy, inflation, financial sector reforms, exchange rate movements and digital financial innovations could be complex, making accurate and accessible reporting important to public understanding. “It is through accurate, balanced, and insightful reporting that these issues are translated into information citizens can understand and use,” he said. The Governor also emphasised the importance of effective communication in central banking, saying public understanding of the Bank’s policies was critical to their effectiveness. “Our policies are most effective when they are clearly understood by the public. Transparency, credibility, and accountability require open and effective engagement with all stakeholders, including the media,” he said. The award forms part of the Bank’s efforts to encourage specialised reporting on economic and financial issues and promote greater public understanding of developments in the sector. It is expected to provide journalists with opportunities to build their reporting skills and deepen their knowledge of issues that affect businesses, households and the wider economy.

items.title: Real Madrid beat Valencia to move level on points with leaders Barcelona
items.description: Real Madrid moved level on points with La Liga leaders Barcelona after a comfortable victory at struggling Valencia. Captain Federico Valverde opened the scoring in the 28th minute with a crisp, low drive from 20 yards after Kylian Mbappe’s free-kick came back off the wall. Eight minutes later, Jose Mourinho’s side doubled their advantage as Arda Guler volleyed in from six yards after Jude Bellingham’s cutback was deflected kindly into his path. The visitors remained in control in the second half and the result was put beyond doubt 15 minutes from time when Guler found Mbappe, who rounded the goalkeeper to score his 13th league goal of the campaign. It only got worse for Valencia as captain Jose Gaya was sent off for scything down Mbappe with the striker set to streak clear on goal. A fourth straight league win means only goal difference keeps Real off top spot, although Barca can restore their three-point advantage when they play third-placed Atletico Madrid on Sunday (20:00 GMT). Valencia stay 19th, a point from safety, after a seventh league defeat from 12 games. The game was paused nine minutes into the first half to allow players and fans to pay tribute to Tenerife striker Jesus de Miguel, who died after suffering a serious injury during a Spanish second-division match, with a minute’s applause.

items.title: Government renews commitment to unravel Ahmed Suale’s murder – Kwakye Ofosu
items.description: The government has reaffirmed its commitment to unraveling the murder of investigative journalist Ahmed Suale, whose killing in January 2019 remains unsolved. Speaking on behalf of President John Dramani Mahama at the 30th GJA Media Awards in Accra, Minister of State in charge of Government Communications, Felix Kwakye Ofosu, said journalists in Ghana had lost their lives in the pursuit of accountability. He cited the killing of Mr Suale, an investigative journalist with Tiger Eye PI, and said the government remained committed to finding those responsible. “Journalists in our country lost their lives in pursuit of accountability, and I refer to the unfortunate killing of Ahmed Suale, whose murder remains unsolved, and the government remains committed to unraveling it,” he stated. Mr Kwakye Ofosu also acknowledged the dangers faced by journalists who publish reports considered uncomfortable by powerful interests. He referred to journalists in the northern part of the country who, he said, had to flee for their lives after publishing such reports. “Our words in support of free speech must not ring hollow, especially when in the north, through the past, journalists had to flee our country for fear of their lives because they published uncomfortable truths,” he stated. Ahmed Suale was shot dead in Madina, Accra, in January 2019. He was part of the Tiger Eye PI investigative team and had worked on investigations into corruption and other matters of public interest. His killing remains unresolved, with the GJA and other media stakeholders continuing to call for justice. The government’s latest pledge comes amid broader concerns about journalist safety and the need to protect media practitioners from intimidation and attacks. Mr Kwakye Ofosu said the government remained committed to pursuing the circumstances surrounding Suale’s murder and protecting journalists across the country.

items.title: Ghana Tennis Federation boss, Aboagye Duah, elected as West Africa Prez & Veep at Tennis Africa
items.description: LUANDA, ANGOLA, 7 November 2026 — Ghana has secured a significant leadership position in African tennis following the election of Mr Isaac Aboagye Duah, President of the Ghana Tennis Federation (GTF), as President of the West Africa Zone and Vice President of Tennis Africa. Mr Duah was elected unopposed at the Tennis Africa Annual General Meeting held in Luanda, Angola, filling the vacancy created by the passing of former Zone President, Ing. Ifedayo Akindoju Dayo, last year. In accordance with the Tennis Africa Constitution, the position was filled through an election at the next AGM. The West Africa Zone comprises 15 countries. Mr Duah’s election presents an opportunity for Ghana to contribute more directly to continental tennis governance and for the sub-region to strengthen cooperation in developing the sport. A Record of Inclusive Leadership Mr Duah has served as President of the Ghana Tennis Federation since 2017. His tenure has focused on inclusive governance, stakeholder engagement, and creating opportunities for the growth of tennis. Two significant initiatives stand out. First, he championed the recognition of players, coaches, officiating officials and clubs as delegates at the highest decision-making body of tennis governance in Ghana, ensuring that key stakeholders have a voice in shaping the sport’s future. Second, he has promoted an open-door policy that creates an enabling environment for tennis clubs and foundations to operate, partner with the Federation and organise internationally recognised World Tennis competitions. Under his leadership, Ghana has participated in West African junior competitions over the past nine years, achieved notable success in African 12-and-under competitions, and continued to represent the country in the Davis Cup and Billie Jean King Cup. Mr Duah also serves on the African Cup of Nations Sub-Committee of Tennis Africa, contributing to the development of continental tennis. A Vision for African Tennis Commenting on his election, Mr Duah said: “I am deeply honoured by the confidence placed in me and humbled by the opportunity to serve tennis across West Africa and the African continent. My leadership philosophy has always been anchored in inclusion, collaboration and the belief that tennis can only grow when players, coaches, officials, clubs and foundations are recognised, valued and given a meaningful voice. “I look forward to bringing this spirit of inclusive leadership to Tennis Africa. Working with our 15 West African member countries and stakeholders across the continent, we can strengthen our institutions, develop our players and officials, attract greater investment and create sustainable opportunities for the next generation. My vision is for an African tennis community that is united in purpose, strong in governance and increasingly competitive on the world stage.” His new responsibilities will provide an opportunity to promote stronger cooperation among national federations, expand junior development, strengthen institutional capacity and encourage investment in tennis infrastructure and competitions. Academic Background Mr Duah is an alumnus of the Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology (KNUST), where he obtained a Bachelor of Science degree in Chemistry. He also holds an Executive Master of Business Administration (EMBA), a Master of Arts in Leadership and Management, and a Chartered Institute of Marketing (CIM-UK) qualification as a Chartered Marketer. He received his secondary education at Pope John Senior High School and Minor Seminary in Koforidua. His election marks an important milestone for Ghanaian sports administration and offers an opportunity to strengthen the country’s contribution to tennis development across West Africa and the continent. The Ghana Tennis Federation congratulates its President on his election and looks forward to his continued service to the sport at both national and continental levels.

items.title: AMERICA IS NOT NIGERIA: Why Trump’s midterm defeat cannot predict Tinubu’s 2027 fortunes
items.description: By Kayode Akinmade The sweeping defeat suffered by President Donald Trump’s Republican Party in the November 3 American midterm elections has predictably provided fresh ammunition for Nigeria’s opposition politicians, who are already attempting to draw parallels between the political fortunes of the American president and those of President Bola Ahmed Tinubu ahead of Nigeria’s 2027 general elections. While the comparison may offer an attractive political talking point, it is, at best, superficial and, at worst, a deliberate attempt to transplant the political circumstances of one country into another. There is no doubt that the Republican defeat represents a significant setback for Trump. Democrats secured control of both chambers of Congress, delivering a powerful electoral rebuke to the Republican administration and signalling widespread dissatisfaction with some of its policies. The result has opened a new chapter in American politics and raised questions about the direction of Trump’s presidency. However, the critical question is whether the circumstances that produced this outcome in the United States are sufficiently comparable to Nigeria’s political and economic realities to justify the conclusion that Tinubu is destined for a similar electoral fate in 2027. The answer is no. America is not Nigeria. Trump is not Tinubu. And the political dynamics of the United States cannot be mechanically imported into Nigeria’s electoral calculations. Indeed, one of the most important factors behind the Republican Party’s defeat was the controversial war involving the United States and Iran, a foreign policy decision that has generated enormous economic, diplomatic and security consequences for the Trump administration. The conflict, which has lasted several months, has heightened concerns about American military involvement abroad, increased pressure on energy markets and contributed to rising fuel prices. For American households already grappling with the cost of living, the war became another source of economic anxiety. Its financial implications, military casualties and uncertain strategic objectives also generated questions about the wisdom of the administration’s foreign policy choices. Iran conflict Significantly, the political consequences were acknowledged by the highest levels of the American government. Trump admitted that the Iran conflict contributed to his party’s electoral difficulties, although he maintained that the military action was necessary. His Vice President, JD Vance, was considerably more direct, declaring that “the reason we lost is the war.” That admission is particularly instructive. It establishes that the Republican defeat was not simply an abstract expression of public dissatisfaction with a sitting president. It was substantially connected to identifiable policy decisions and their consequences for American voters. The question, therefore, is why Nigeria’s opposition should expect the political consequences of Trump’s decision to engage Iran to automatically translate into an electoral liability for Tinubu. Nigeria did not initiate the conflict. Tinubu did not authorise American military operations against Iran. He does not determine American foreign policy, the direction of Trump’s trade tariffs or the domestic political calculations of the Republican Party. To suggest that the electoral consequences of these decisions constitute a direct verdict on Nigeria’s president is to stretch political analogy beyond its reasonable limits. Of course, the opposition is entitled to draw lessons from developments elsewhere. Political parties routinely study elections in other countries, particularly when they reveal the relationship between public expectations, government performance and electoral accountability. But learning from another country’s political experience is fundamentally different from assuming that its electoral outcome must be replicated elsewhere. There is an even more important distinction that deserves attention: the American midterm elections are not presidential elections. The midterms are held halfway through the president’s four-year tenure and determine the composition of Congress. They frequently become a referendum on the sitting president and his party, as voters use the opportunity to express satisfaction or dissatisfaction with the administration. Historically, the party controlling the White House has often faced considerable losses during midterm elections. Nigeria’s 2027 general election, by contrast, will be a presidential contest in which voters will choose the individual and political party they believe are best equipped to govern the country for another four years. The candidates will have to present their records, programmes, leadership credentials and policy alternatives before the Nigerian electorate. The difference is fundamental. A congressional election in the United States, influenced by a controversial foreign war, cannot automatically become a reliable predictor of a presidential election in Nigeria. But beyond the political comparison, there is a more substantive issue that Nigeria’s opposition must confront: the country’s economic circumstances and the choices available to any government seeking to address them. Structural weaknesses Nigeria’s economic difficulties did not begin on May 29, 2023. The country entered the Tinubu administration with longstanding structural weaknesses, including an expensive petrol subsidy regime, multiple exchange-rate arrangements, weak revenue mobilisation, infrastructure deficits, excessive dependence on imports and a productive sector constrained by years of economic distortions. These challenges accumulated over successive administrations and progressively reduced the government’s fiscal room for manoeuvre. The new administration decided to confront some of these problems through the removal of petrol subsidy, foreign exchange reforms, fiscal restructuring and efforts to improve domestic revenue generation. These were not politically convenient decisions. Neither were they painless. Millions of Nigerians have experienced considerable hardship since the introduction of the reforms. The rising cost of food, transportation, electricity and other essential services has placed enormous pressure on households and businesses. No credible assessment of the Tinubu administration can ignore this reality, and no amount of economic statistics should be deployed to dismiss the daily struggles of ordinary citizens. However, the existence of hardship does not eliminate the need to examine the structural problems that necessitated reform in the first place. What would have happened if the government had continued to finance an increasingly expensive subsidy regime without addressing the distortions it created? What would have been the consequences of maintaining multiple exchange rates and the associated opportunities for arbitrage? Could Nigeria have continued accumulating fiscal liabilities while expecting its economy to become more competitive and attractive to investors? These are legitimate questions that the opposition must answer if it wishes to present a credible alternative. The more important issue is not simply whether the reforms have imposed hardship. It is whether they are correcting the structural weaknesses of the economy, whether implementation is sufficiently effective and whether the government is doing enough to ensure that the benefits eventually reach ordinary Nigerians. There are already indicators suggesting that the Nigerian economy is experiencing some improvement in its macroeconomic fundamentals. The Federal Ministry of Finance’s macroeconomic dashboard reported real GDP growth of 4.43 per cent in the second quarter of 2026, compared with 4.23 per cent in the corresponding period of 2025. Headline inflation declined to 15.39 per cent in August 2026 from 23.14 per cent a year earlier. External reserves also rose to approximately $54.7 billion as of September 18, 2026. Federation Account revenue increased from approximately N15.2 trillion in 2024 to N21.9 trillion in 2025, representing an increase of about 44 per cent. These figures provide evidence of improved revenue mobilisation and strengthening external buffers. They are significant developments in an economy that previously struggled with severe revenue constraints and foreign exchange pressures. Context Nevertheless, these improvements must be understood within their proper context. A decline in inflation does not mean that prices have returned to previous levels. It means that the rate at which prices are increasing has slowed. Similarly, stronger foreign reserves and increased government revenues do not automatically translate into improved purchasing power for households. The real challenge for the Tinubu administration is to convert these macroeconomic gains into tangible improvements in the lives of Nigerians. This requires more affordable food, improved electricity supply, lower production costs, better security, employment opportunities and stronger social protection for vulnerable citizens. It is here that the government must concentrate its attention as the 2027 elections approach. The administration’s performance must also be assessed beyond the immediate cost-of-living debate. Its infrastructure programme, investments in transportation, efforts to strengthen food production, reforms in the education sector and initiatives to improve the business environment are all relevant components of national development. Projects such as the Lagos-Calabar Coastal Highway and the Sokoto-Badagry Superhighway reflect the administration’s ambition to expand strategic transport infrastructure and improve national connectivity. Their ultimate value, however, must be measured by delivery, quality, economic impact and the benefits they provide to communities and businesses. Governance is multidimensional. A country’s economic performance cannot be reduced to the price of a bag of rice, just as the success of an administration cannot be established merely by announcing infrastructure projects. Both household welfare and long-term national development must form part of a balanced assessment. This brings the discussion to the responsibility of the opposition. Democracy requires a credible opposition capable of questioning government policies, exposing shortcomings and offering alternative solutions. The economic difficulties facing Nigerians provide legitimate grounds for robust political scrutiny. The opposition should therefore be encouraged to challenge the government and present its own vision for the country’s future. But criticism alone is not a governing programme. Beyond celebrating Trump’s electoral setback, Nigerians deserve to know what the opposition intends to do differently. Would it restore petrol subsidy, and how would it finance such an arrangement sustainably? Would it return to the multiple exchange-rate system? What practical measures would it introduce to reduce inflation, improve food security, strengthen the naira, attract investment and create employment? How would it finance the infrastructure Nigeria urgently needs without returning the country to unsustainable borrowing and fiscal practices? These are not unreasonable questions. They are the minimum requirements of a serious political alternative. The opposition cannot expect to win the confidence of Nigerians simply by drawing attention to the electoral difficulties of a foreign president. Nor can the Republican Party’s defeat serve as a substitute for a Nigerian economic manifesto. There is also a lesson for the ruling APC. The American experience demonstrates that political loyalty, electoral victories and presidential popularity cannot be taken for granted. Voters ultimately respond to their lived experiences, expectations and perceptions of government performance. The fact that an administration considers its policies necessary does not automatically mean that citizens will accept the consequences indefinitely. Communicating achievements Tinubu and the APC must therefore understand that the 2027 election cannot be won merely by explaining why the reforms were necessary. The government must demonstrate what those reforms are delivering. It must communicate its achievements more effectively, address areas of public dissatisfaction and ensure that economic recovery becomes visible in the everyday lives of Nigerians. The administration must also resist the temptation to dismiss legitimate criticism as opposition propaganda. Nigerians who are struggling with food prices, transportation costs, insecurity and unemployment are not necessarily political opponents. They are citizens whose concerns deserve attention and practical responses. Ultimately, the 2027 election will be a contest of records, ideas, leadership capacity and public confidence. Tinubu will have to defend his administration’s performance, while the opposition will have to demonstrate that it possesses a more credible and workable alternative. The American midterm elections may offer useful lessons about the consequences of unpopular policies and the importance of public accountability. But they cannot determine the outcome of Nigeria’s presidential election. American voters have made their choice based on American circumstances. Nigerians will make theirs based on their own experiences and expectations. The attempt to turn Trump’s defeat into a prediction of Tinubu’s political future may generate headlines and energise opposition conversations, but it does not settle the more important questions about Nigeria’s economic direction and political choices. The burden of persuasion rests on both sides. The government must demonstrate results, and the opposition must demonstrate capacity. In the final analysis, America will judge Trump, just as Nigeria will judge Tinubu. Neither president can borrow the electoral fortunes or misfortunes of the other. America is not Nigeria. Trump is not Tinubu. And the road to Nigeria’s 2027 presidential election will be determined not in Washington, but by the choices of Nigerians. The post AMERICA IS NOT NIGERIA: Why Trump’s midterm defeat cannot predict Tinubu’s 2027 fortunes appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Countdown to 2027: Edo North is for Oshiomhole
items.description: By Allison Abanum Adams Oshiomhole’s first term has been defined by a deliberate strategy of translating legislative power into tangible federal presence for Edo North. As Chairman of the Senate Committee on Interior, he has leveraged his position to facilitate federal employment for constituents and ensure fair representation in federal institutions. His legislative record includes moving over 10 motions and sponsoring many bills. These are not abstract motions; they are institutional investments that will outlast any single political cycle. On the ground, Oshiomhole constituency interventions have reached all wards in Edo North, a coverage rate that speaks to both reach and intentionality. Oshiomhole has moved from delivering roads to delivering accountability, and Edo North have seen the difference in both bricks and budgets. Beyond infrastructure, his engagement with youth leaders and traditional rulers signals a recognition that representation must be relational, not transactional, a point underscored by his refusal to charge constituents for assistance and his warning against extortion in his name. The political consolidation around Oshiomhole 2027 bid reflects a broader strategic calculation within Edo North. Endorsements have since crossed traditional lines: From the market women in Auchi to the Artisan in Iyahmo, down to all the student bodies and community leaders, it is clear that it is no longer a question of whether Edo North is standing for Oshiomhole; it is a question of how loudly Edo North will say so. To the people in the rural areas of Edo North, they have risen from service, unity, and discipline: delivery that touches households, reconciliation that silences internal friction, and grassroots organisation that turns intention into votes. The good people of Edo North on their own are moving ward by ward to get support for Oshiomhole. The plough is heavy; the hands must be steady because the furrow ahead is 2027. The message is clear: no retreat, no sideways glance, no nostalgia for old battles in Edo North. A senatorial district that has seen the light and future must now prove it can cultivate it, row by row, ward by ward, state by state, until the harvest of triumph is achieved. Every leader, every member, every supporter keeps eyes on the furrow, not on the noise. So, let the word go forth: APC is on the plough, and there is no looking back until Oshiomhole is sent back to the Senate in 2027. The task is not to boast of yesterday but to labour for tomorrow with humility, focus, and determination. The harvest belongs to those who keep ploughing. For a senatorial district that has historically oscillated between alignment and agitation, the emerging consensus is that Oshiomhole federal network is an asset too valuable to surrender. Abanum lives in Abuja. The post Countdown to 2027: Edo North is for Oshiomhole appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Government does not expect favourable headlines from media – Kwakye Ofosu
items.description: The government has reaffirmed its commitment to media freedom, saying it does not expect favourable headlines from journalists as a condition for engagement with the media. Speaking on behalf of President John Dramani Mahama at the 30th GJA Media Awards in Accra, Minister of State in charge of Government Communications, Felix Kwakye Ofosu, said the media must be free to question government, scrutinise public expenditure, investigate public institutions and examine decisions taken by public officials. He said the government recognises that a democratic administration must be prepared to respond to difficult questions and accept legitimate criticism. “We do not expect favourable headlines as a condition for engagement, nor do we expect journalists to surrender their editorial independence in the name of partnership. Indeed, a government that is confident in its democratic credentials must be prepared to answer difficult questions and accept legitimate criticism,” he stated. Mr Kwakye Ofosu said journalists must be allowed to criticise government when it falls short, acknowledge achievements when they are delivered and demand explanations whenever the public interest requires it. “The media must be free to criticise whenever there’s a shortfall, acknowledge achievements when we deliver, and demand explanations whenever the public interest requires it,” he said. The Minister also highlighted the need to protect journalists from attacks, threats and unlawful detention while carrying out their professional duties. He said allegations of attacks, including those involving security personnel, must be investigated and accountability pursued where wrongdoing is established. “No journalist should be assaulted, threatened, or unlawfully detained for undertaking a legitimate professional assignment. Allegations of attacks, including those involving security personnel, must be investigated, and where wrongdoing is established, accountability must follow,” he stated. The comments come amid concerns about the safety of journalists and the state of media freedom in Ghana. The Ghana Journalists Association (GJA) has recorded more than 50 incidents involving attacks, arrests and harassment of journalists between 2022 and January 2026. The government says it will continue to work with media stakeholders to ensure that constitutional guarantees of freedom of expression and media independence are reflected in the everyday experiences of journalists.

items.title: A Ballot on a Burial Date? Northern Nigeria Confronts the Symbolism of January 16
items.description: By Hassan A Karofi The choice of dates in politics is often presented as a matter of administrative convenience. Yet history teaches us that dates carry powerful symbolism, especially in societies where collective memories of tragedy and triumph remain deeply rooted. As Nigeria prepares for a presidential election scheduled for January 16, 2026, it is important to reflect on what that date means to millions of people, particularly in Northern Nigeria, where January 16 is associated with one of the darkest episodes in the country’s history. The significance of January 16 cannot be understood without revisiting the events of the country’s first military coup. In the early hours of January 15, 1966, a group of young military officers launched Nigeria’s first coup d’état. By the morning of January 16, the consequences of the coup were evident. Several of Nigeria’s most prominent political and military leaders had been assassinated. Among those killed were Sir Ahmadu Bello, the Sardauna of Sokoto and Premier of Northern Nigeria; Sir Abubakar Tafawa Balewa, Nigeria’s first Prime Minister; Brigadier Samuel Ademulegun; Brigadier Zakariya Maimalari; and other senior political and military figures. While leaders from different regions were affected, the perception in the North was that the coup disproportionately targeted Northern political leadership. This perception would profoundly shape political attitudes and inter-ethnic relations for decades. The events following the coup further deepened Northern grievances. Major General Johnson Aguiyi-Ironsi assumed power and suspended parts of the constitutional order. In many parts of Northern Nigeria, suspicion and anger grew rapidly, culminating in the counter-coup of July 1966. The resulting instability ultimately contributed to the chain of events that led to the Nigerian Civil War. More than six decades later, the memory of January 1966 remains alive. For many Northern families, historians, traditional institutions, and political observers, January 16 is not merely another date on the calendar. It is a reminder of a traumatic turning point that altered Nigeria’s political trajectory and claimed the lives of leaders who continue to be revered across the region. Against this backdrop, the decision to hold a presidential election on January 16 raises legitimate questions. Whether the date was chosen for logistical, constitutional, or electoral reasons, policymakers should recognize that symbolism matters in politics. Elections are national events meant to unite citizens around a shared democratic purpose. When an election coincides with a date associated with historical mourning for a significant section of the country, there is a risk that the symbolism overshadows the democratic exercise itself. This concern is not necessarily about rejecting the election or questioning its legitimacy. Rather, it is about understanding how political decisions are perceived. In diverse societies such as Nigeria, sensitivity to historical memory is an important component of nation-building. Governments regularly avoid scheduling major celebrations on dates associated with national tragedies. The same principle can reasonably be applied to major political events. There is also the risk of misinterpretation. In an era of social media, symbolism can quickly become politicized. Political actors may exploit the coincidence to revive old grievances, reinforce regional narratives, or deepen distrust among communities. What may have been intended as a neutral administrative decision could inadvertently reopen historical wounds. Supporters of the January 16 date may argue that Nigeria cannot permanently suspend public activities because of historical anniversaries. They may also point out that democracy requires adherence to electoral timelines regardless of symbolism. These arguments deserve consideration. However, they do not eliminate the responsibility to assess whether alternative dates could achieve the same constitutional objectives without generating unnecessary controversy. A mature democracy is not only defined by the conduct of elections but also by sensitivity to the historical experiences of its citizens. The memory of the January 1966 coup remains a significant part of Northern Nigeria’s political consciousness. For many, the date symbolizes loss, betrayal, and the beginning of a national crisis from which the country took years to recover. As Nigeria continues its democratic journey, leaders should remember that national unity is strengthened when historical sensitivities are acknowledged rather than dismissed. The question is therefore not whether an election can legally be held on January 16. The more important question is whether it is politically wise and symbolically appropriate to do so. History may not dictate the future, but ignoring its lessons often comes at a cost. For many in Northern Nigeria, January 16 remains a day of remembrance. Policymakers would do well to reflect on whether a date synonymous with mourning is the right day for a defining national political contest. *Karofi can be reached via hassankarofi@yahoo.com The post A Ballot on a Burial Date? Northern Nigeria Confronts the Symbolism of January 16 appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: 2027: Between Okowa and Ochei, a Trojan horse race?
items.description: By Emmanuel l. Nwagboniwe Let’s not equivocate here. The indices and optics in the political space amply suggest that the electoral race to represent Delta North in the Senate in 2027 is a direct contest between the former Delta State Governor, Dr. Ifeanyi Okowa of the All Progressives Congress (APC ), and ex -Speaker of the Delta State House of Assembly, Victor Ochei of the National Democratic Party (NDC). Evidently, the projection of a contest likely to throw up soap- box rhetoric, anxieties, euphoria, and political high drama, horse trading, and possibly, mudslinging, is a no-brainer: Okowa and Ochei have bounced into the political ring with unequalled superlatives and robust social capital. Commendably too, these former political allies’ ‘roll call of honour’ tells a convincing story of remarkably impressive private and public service careers- years put in and sacrificed largely in selfless and people-centred engagements. For instance, a studied glance at Dr Ifeanyi Okowa’s resume speaks volumes: medical doctor; council chairman; Commissioner of Health; Secretary to the Delta State Government (SSG); Senator of the Federal Republic of Nigeria; two- term Governor of Delta State, ex -Vice Presidential candidate of the People’s Democratic Party (PDP) in the 2023 General Election. Conversely, Victor Ochei is equally a no fresher in the public cum political space. He is a graduate of Chemical Engineering; Founder/ Chairman of Day Notch Nigeria Limited, an engineering firm of global status; Member, Delta State House of Assembly representing Aniocha North Council; Deputy Minority Leader; Speaker, Delta State House of Assembly; Executive Director, Maritime Labour and Cabotage Services at the Nigerian Maritime Administration and Safety Agency (NlMASA); President, Nigerian Tennis Federation, among others. Without gas lighting, these political highflyers’ ‘selling points’ make any of them eminently qualified to represent the Anioma nationality in the Red Chamber. However, one knows that making a choice out of these two top contenders, especially by voters in a dynamic and highly unpredictable democratic space like ours where selfish and primordial sentiments hold sway, is certainly a herculean task, yet a candidate’s ‘report card’ remains an added advantage. For Okowa, he is majorly regarded as a grassroots politician who walks his talk in terms of mass mobilisation, especially across the nine councils that make up the Delta North Senatorial District. Evidently too, the former governor’s enduring stay in the political trenches for over three decades tells a reassuring story of one who understands the undercurrents and dynamics of power ‘capture’. Moreover, Okowa has other political assets to take to the electioneering field; he has a vast and extensive experience in the executive and the legislative arms of government, and no matter how hard his traducers knock him, he being an ex -state executive, has a chunk of tangible and verifiable score cards to present to his Delta North constituents. As the campaigns intensify, he will readily reel out the dividends of democracy he provided as a sitting governor to his Delta North voters. Even his consultative town hall meetings have been turned into endorsements of sorts by traditional institutions -though an exercise dismissed by Ochei’s camp as a mere smokescreen in a democratic dispensation anchored on one man, one vote mantra. Moreover, for a political strongman believed largely to be an ‘Establishment’ candidate, Okowa would be waging a double barreled war against his contenders, as he will leverage not only on the state government’s mobilisation drive, but most likely as well as from its near inelastic financial muscle. Truth is: Okowa’s opponents must be ready to deepen their resource base to be able to match him in the battle royale for the exalted Abuja seat. At this juncture, therefore, one is tempted to ask: Are Okowa’s intimidating credentials and robust service- delivery profile over the years enough pointers to cow any of his opponents to throw in the towel and make a cautious and timely retreat from the political battle field. In other words, can Ochei, a major contender, continue to tackle a man who has withered various political storms, tempest and near deadly intrigues? Well, feelers one gets from those who know Ochei closely say, he is not one who easily runs away from political battles, many others describe him as a human dynamo and an incurable optimist who dares where even angels thread softly. Moreover, he is coming to the electioneering arena with a dose of youthful dynamism and vibrancy. At 57, Ochei is believed to leverage on his mass appeal among the youths, as his message of generational shift in leadership resonates far and wide in the nine councils of Delta North. He and his teeming supporters are already taking a swipe at Okowa for allegedly foisting a clandestine political dynasty for his family and cronies. Still, Ochei who flaunts his impressive performance as a former lawmaker for Aniocha North echoes that his mission to the Senate is to replicate that same feat in the entire Delta North, insisting he has the capacity and political sagacity to attract federal presence to Anioma land more than any other candidate. Ochei and his supporters are equally taking his redemptive message to town, affirming that he is on a rescue mission, to bridge what they call the ‘huge infrastructural decay’ in Delta North despite the zone’s role in the electoral victory of the now APC -led administration in the State. In his resolute bid to actualise his vision at the Senate if elected, Ochei has rolled out a 10 -point Agenda encapsulated in an all- inclusive governance, better security, power, job opportunities, infrastructure, agriculture, productivity, among others. Also, the former Speaker is latching onto the integrity and impeccable qualities of his party’s Presidential candidate, Mr. Peter Obi, to drive his message of redemption home. Moreover, the NDC flag bearer is making much capital from what he regards as the ‘suffocating hardship’ in the country occasioned by the removal of fuel subsidy by the APC- led federal government ,to market his candidacy. Well, as the January 16, 2027 polls draws nearer, the most pertinent questions on many lips are: Between Okowa and Ochei, who blinks first? Can Ochei, a candidate described by Okowa’s many supporters as a feather weight, pull a surprise, and possibly upstage the steely ex-governor in the electoral contest? Or will the enigmatic Okowa clinch the coveted Senate seat seamlessly? Well, let’s not beat our chest in certainty as to which direction the political pendulum will swing towards, after all the projections and permutations here are mere conjectures buried in the womb of time. •Nwagboniwe, a journalist, writes from Lagos. The post 2027: Between Okowa and Ochei, a Trojan horse race? appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: FG plans National Sports Commission office in Kwara – Magaji
items.description: By Demola Akinyemi ILORIN – The Federal Government has concluded plans to establish an office of the National Sports Commission (NSC) in Kwara State, following the development of sports facilities by the administration of Governor AbdulRahman AbdulRazaq. The Executive Chairman of the Kwara State Sports Commission, Coach Bola Magaji, disclosed this in Ilorin, saying officials of the NSC had been impressed by the facilities provided by the state government. Magaji spoke at the unveiling of a book titled The Sardauna of Ilorin in the Eyes of History, written in honour of AbdulRazaq, who holds the traditional title of Sardauna of Ilorin. The book was authored by Abiodun Abdul Kareem, a senior journalist and editor of Herald on Sunday, the Sunday publication of the Kwara State Printing and Publishing Corporation. Magaji recalled that officials of the National Sports Commission visited Kwara about three weeks ago to assess the sports facilities developed by the AbdulRazaq administration over the past seven years. He said the officials expressed satisfaction with the facilities at the state stadium complex and indicated that the proposed NSC office would be established in the state. According to him, the development reflects the growing recognition of Kwara’s investment in sports infrastructure. Magaji said the state’s stadium complex could boast of some of the best squash court facilities in the world, adding that Kwara contingents to national and international sporting competitions had recorded improved medal-winning performances. He attributed the development to investments in sports infrastructure and efforts to promote sporting activities in the state. Also speaking, the Special Adviser and Counsellor to the Governor, Alhaji Saad Salahudeen, said AbdulRazaq’s contributions to governance, politics, youth development and national development would continue to attract attention in the years ahead. He said the governor’s footprints in public service would remain relevant and be referenced in the next 50 years. Earlier, the Chairman of the Organising Committee, Mallam Umar Abdulwahab, said the event was designed to provide a platform for discussions on leadership, public service, governance and historical preservation. He said the initiative was also aimed at documenting experiences and inspiring future generations. The event was attended by several dignitaries, including the Emir of Ilorin, Alhaji Ibrahim Sulu-Gambari, who was represented by Magaji Ogundele; Alhaji Saad Kajola; Alhaji Yusuf Abdullahi; the Secretary to the State Government, Professor Mamman Jibril; Senior Adviser on Islamic Religion, Alhaji Ibrahim Danmegoro; and Senior Adviser on Political Communication, Alhaji Bashir Adigun, among others.
